 Portable power stations are useful for everything from keeping your broadband running during a power cut to powering equipment away from a convenient socket. The Anker Solix S2000 fits both roles, combining a substantial battery with a relatively compact upright design.
 What impressed me most, though, was how little fuss it involved. It handled repeated sessions with a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum straight out of the box, while the accompanying app was easy to set up and refreshingly clear about what its settings actually do.

 Design and connections 
 The S2000 has an understated appearance: a dark grey enclosure, rounded edges and a glossy front panel. It looks perfectly at home beside a desk, although mine was soon earning its keep around DIY equipment.
 Its upright shape gives it a reasonably small footprint. At 16.2kg, however, “portable” still involves a deliberate lift. Moving it between rooms or taking it out to the garden is one thing; carrying it a long distance is another.
 The UK version has four proper Type G sockets, split evenly between the front and rear. That arrangement makes sense. You can keep regularly connected equipment plugged in behind the unit, leaving the front sockets available for things you connect occasionally.
 There is a trade-off: you’ll need access to both sides if you want to use every socket. Bear that in mind before squeezing it into a tight space, and leave the ventilation clear.

 The USB connections sit above the display. The 100W USB-C port is the one to choose for a compatible laptop, while the other USB-C connection is limited to 15W. They look similar, so it’s worth checking the labels.
 The screen puts the remaining battery percentage front and centre, alongside input and output wattage and an estimated remaining time. That gives you the information you need without reaching for your phone.
 Performance: a proper day’s work 
 My S2000 arrived with a 59% state of charge. Rather than charging it fully before doing anything useful, I put it straight to work powering a 1,200W wet/dry vacuum.
 Between approximately 10am and 5pm, I used the vacuum repeatedly in sessions lasting around five to ten minutes. The Anker handled those sessions without any problems, and by the time I finished, it still showed 13% remaining.
 To be clear, that was intermittent use across a seven-hour working day, rather than seven hours of continuous vacuuming. Even so, it was a useful practical test: repeated use of a fairly demanding appliance, starting with little more than half a battery.
 The benefit was simple. I could get on with the job without running an extension lead back to a mains socket, and the power station had enough charge to cover the work I needed to do.
 This wasn’t a controlled capacity test. I didn’t record the vacuum’s total running time or measure the energy delivered at the socket, so it wouldn’t be fair to calculate an efficiency figure from the percentage drop.
 What I can say is that it coped comfortably with this particular vacuum and pattern of use.
 The main limitation is the 1,500W continuous output. Battery capacity tells you how much energy is stored; output determines which appliances it can run. A large battery doesn’t automatically mean it can power a typical high-wattage UK kettle or several demanding tools together.
 Check appliance ratings, allow for starting demands, and remember that the output limit is shared across the AC sockets.
 Charging options 
 (Image credit: Future) For everyday charging, the S2000 connects directly to the mains using the supplied AC cable. There’s no separate external power brick to find space for.
 During one charging session, the front display showed approximately 1,068W going in. An app screenshot taken during charging showed around 1,077W, with UltraFast charging switched off. These are snapshots rather than a timed charging test, but they show a substantial charging rate in normal use.
 There’s also an app-controlled UltraFast option when a quicker turnaround matters.
 Away from home, the S2000 supports compatible solar panels and vehicle charging, provided you have the correct cables and accessories. Solar input is capped at 400W, with Anker specifying a maximum open-circuit voltage of 60V. Panel compatibility matters as well as the connector.
 Those alternatives add flexibility, although a normal car accessory socket will be much slower than mains charging. Think of it as a way to replenish charge while travelling, rather than expecting a quick refill of a 2kWh battery.
 The app: easy to set up, easy to understand 
 (Image credit: Future || Anker) The app was one of the nicest surprises.
 Finding it in the Google Play Store was straightforward, as were signing in and getting started. The S2000 was detected straight away, added without difficulty and ready to control. An iPhone version also appears to be available, although my experience here was with Android.
 The main screen presents the battery percentage, temperature, charging estimate and power flow clearly. You can see what’s happening at a glance.
 More useful still is the depth of control. There are multiple UPS and power-management modes, charging timers, adjustable AC charging power and battery charge limits. You also get AC output scheduling, a countdown to switch the sockets off, screen controls and power-usage history.
 Crucially, the explanations are good. Rather than leaving you to decipher a vaguely named mode, the app helps you understand what a setting does and decide whether it suits your needs.
 Some power-station apps make configuration feel like educated guesswork. Here, the guidance makes the extra features more approachable, particularly if this is your first battery system.
 Backup power and everyday use 
 The UPS function adds another potential role: keeping suitable equipment powered when the mains fails. Anker quotes a transfer time of around 10ms, although I haven’t independently measured that or tested compatibility with individual computers.
 For a home office, the combination of rear sockets, battery monitoring and configurable operating modes is appealing. You can leave equipment connected and manage the unit without constantly handling it.

 Last updated: October 16, 2026 · Reviewed for U.S. home-backup use, transfer-switch compatibility, voltage limitations, backfeed safety, and current UDPOWER specifications.
 Quick answer: Can you connect a portable power station to a transfer switch? 
 Yes, some portable power stations can supply selected home circuits through a properly matched transfer switch. But the power station, inlet, transfer equipment, voltage, amperage, neutral/ground configuration, and the circuits being backed up all have to be compatible.
 A 120V-only portable power station cannot become a 120/240V split-phase source just because it is connected to a 30A or 50A generator transfer switch. If the station only provides 120V, your backup plan should normally be limited to compatible 120V loads unless the equipment manufacturer and a licensed electrician specifically approve another configuration.
 Never connect a portable power station to a wall outlet, dryer outlet, or other household receptacle in an attempt to backfeed the electrical panel. 
 How Does a Transfer Switch Work With a Portable Power Station?
 A portable power station normally powers appliances directly from the AC outlets built into the unit. That works well for a refrigerator, router, CPAP machine, laptop, TV, lamp, or other plug-in equipment.
 The situation changes when you want to power something that is part of the home's wiring. Ceiling lights, some furnaces, sump pumps, permanently wired appliances, and normal wall receptacles are supplied through the electrical panel rather than through an extension cord.
 A transfer switch provides a controlled way to choose which source feeds a circuit: normal utility power or approved backup power.
 1. Portable power station 
Provides the backup AC power.
 2. Approved connection method 
Connects the backup source to transfer equipment using equipment that matches the source voltage, current, plug type, and installation.
 3. Transfer switch 
Separates the utility source from the backup source so they are not unintentionally connected together.
 4. Selected household circuits 
Receive backup power within the limits of the power station and transfer equipment.
 This is fundamentally different from plugging a power station into a household receptacle. A properly installed transfer system controls the power path; backfeeding through an ordinary wall outlet does not.
 Why this matters: Transfer equipment is designed to prevent utility power and backup power from being connected together unintentionally. That isolation helps protect the home, the backup equipment, and utility workers restoring service. The Electrical Safety Foundation International and transfer-switch manufacturers such as Generac specifically warn against directly backfeeding household wiring.
 The Five Compatibility Checks That Matter
 The question is not simply, “Does my power station have enough watts?” A transfer-switch setup has several separate compatibility requirements. Passing four out of five is not enough.
 Compatibility Check 
 What to Confirm 
 Why It Matters 
 Common Mistake 
 Voltage 
 120V only or true 120/240V split-phase output 
 The source voltage must match the circuits being supplied. 
 Assuming an adapter can turn 120V into 240V. 
 Continuous output 
 Total rated watts and available AC current 
 The selected circuits must stay within the power station's normal output capability. 
 Sizing from surge or peak watts instead of rated output.

 A 120V household outlet is not automatically compatible with a 125/250V L14-30 transfer inlet. 
 Buying an adapter solely because the connectors physically fit.

 Different transfer switches treat the neutral differently, and an incorrect configuration can create faults or nuisance trips. 
 Assuming all battery power stations have the same neutral configuration.

 The home wiring has to be compatible with the source as well as the switch. 
 Choosing circuits only by appliance running watts. 
 1. Match the voltage first
 This is the fastest way to eliminate an incompatible setup.
 If a portable power station provides only 120V AC, it is fundamentally a 120V source. It can be useful for many important household loads, but it does not provide the two opposite 120V legs used to create 240V in a typical U.S. residential electrical system.
 That means a 120V-only station should not be expected to run 240V equipment such as most central air-conditioning systems, electric clothes dryers, large electric water heaters, electric ranges, Level 2 EV charging equipment, or many deep-well pumps.
 2. Use rated output for system planning
 Transfer-switch planning should be based on the station's normal rated output, not simply the largest number printed in a surge or higher-power mode specification.
 For example, a 2,400W power station operating at 120V represents approximately:
 2,400W ÷ 120V = 20A 
 Connecting that station to transfer equipment rated for 30A does not suddenly give the station 30A of continuous power. The source remains the limiting factor.
 Useful rule: A transfer switch's amp rating tells you what the switch can handle. It does not tell you how much electricity the portable power station can produce.
 3. The plug and inlet must actually be designed for each other
 Many traditional generator transfer switches use a 30A L14-30 inlet or a 50A 125/250V inlet because they are designed for generators that provide 120/240V split-phase power.
 For example, Reliance Controls lists its R310A transfer switch as a 125/250V, 30A unit with an L14-30 inlet .
 That specification is materially different from a 120V-only portable power station with ordinary household-style AC receptacles.
 There are also transfer products designed specifically for 120/125V applications. Reliance, for example, lists a 125V, 15A single-circuit transfer switch intended for loads such as a forced-air furnace and capable of accepting backup power from generators, inverters, and other standby sources.
 The lesson is simple: choose transfer equipment around the actual power source, not the other way around. 
 4. Neutral and ground configuration cannot be guessed
 This is one of the biggest differences between connecting an appliance directly and connecting backup power to household wiring.
 Some transfer switches switch the neutral. Others do not. Some backup sources have a bonded neutral, while others use a floating arrangement. GFCI-protected outputs can also behave differently depending on the transfer equipment.
 You do not need to become an electrician to own a portable power station. You do need the electrician installing or reviewing the transfer equipment to confirm how the specific power station, inlet, transfer switch, grounding system, and branch circuits work together.
 5. Check the circuits, not just the appliances
 A refrigerator may be a 120V appliance, but the circuit feeding it may also serve other outlets. A furnace blower may run on 120V but have a large startup requirement. A pump may look manageable by running wattage but draw much more while starting.
 Before choosing the circuits you want to back up, record:
 circuit voltage;
 breaker rating;
 normal running watts;
 motor or compressor startup demand;
 whether other loads share the circuit;
 whether the circuit uses AFCI or GFCI protection;
 whether it is part of a shared-neutral or multi-wire branch circuit;
 whether the load is hardwired or plug-connected.
 If startup power is unfamiliar, see What Does Surge Current Mean? for a practical explanation of running current, inrush current, compressor startup, and motor loads.

 A large battery capacity does not automatically make a portable power station suitable for every home circuit. Voltage is a separate limitation.

 Manual transfer switches are often the simplest concept
 A manual transfer switch lets you decide when selected circuits change from utility power to the backup source. There is no assumption that the battery automatically powers the entire home.
 That makes selected-circuit backup particularly sensible for a finite battery. Instead of trying to imitate normal grid usage, you can reserve energy for refrigeration, communications, lighting, a furnace blower, or other priorities.
 Automatic transfer does not automatically mean compatible
 Some larger home-battery ecosystems offer proprietary automatic or smart transfer equipment. Those systems are designed around specific power stations, voltages, communication systems, and output connectors.
 A general-purpose portable power station should not be assumed to support an automatic transfer switch simply because both products use AC electricity.
 What Household Circuits Should You Actually Put on Battery Backup?
 The best battery transfer-switch plan is usually not the plan with the most circuits. It is the one that preserves your battery for the loads that matter.
 A practical priority order for many homes is:
 Medical or essential personal equipment
 Refrigerator or freezer
 Internet equipment and phone charging
 Essential lighting
 Heating-system controls or a compatible furnace blower
 Sump pump where applicable
 Limited convenience outlets
 Short-duration cooking loads only when adequate power remains
 For a more complete outage priority plan, see Power Priorities: What to Run First During a Power Outage .
 Loads that are usually poor battery priorities
 Even when an appliance technically fits within the inverter rating, it may consume battery energy so quickly that it is a poor outage choice.

 How Big Should the Portable Power Station Be?
 There are three different numbers to check:
 Voltage: Does the power source provide the voltage the circuit requires?
 Watts: Can the inverter support the highest simultaneous load?
 Watt-hours: Does the battery hold enough energy for the runtime you want?
 Do not confuse watts and watt-hours. A 2,400W inverter rating tells you how much load the station can support at one time. A 2,083Wh battery rating tells you roughly how much stored energy is available.
 For UDPOWER planning examples, a practical estimate uses approximately 90% conversion efficiency:
 Estimated runtime ≈ battery capacity × 0.90 ÷ average load watts 
 If you want a more detailed home-sizing framework, see What Size Solar Generator Do You Need to Power a House? .
 Do not add every breaker rating together
 Suppose a transfer switch contains four 15A circuits. That does not mean your power station must provide 60A. Breaker ratings are circuit protection limits, not a prediction that every circuit continuously draws its maximum current.
 What matters to the battery system is the actual simultaneous load .
 If a refrigerator is using 90W on average, a router is using 20W, several LED lights total 40W, and a laptop is drawing 65W, the approximate running load is only 215W before considering appliance cycling and startup events.

 A transfer switch does not increase battery capacity. Once household circuits are connected, it is actually easier to consume energy without noticing because devices behave like they normally do.

Any connection to home transfer equipment should first be evaluated by a licensed electrician for voltage, circuit selection, inlet compatibility, neutral/ground configuration, protective devices, and local code requirements.

 If you do not need hardwired circuits, direct appliance connection is often simpler. You avoid paying for transfer equipment, and you can see exactly what is plugged into the battery.
 Browse the full UDPOWER portable power station collection or the portable power stations for home backup .
 Why a Transfer Switch Can Actually Make Battery Management Harder
 This is an important difference between a battery and a gasoline generator.
 A fuel generator can be refueled. A portable battery starts with a fixed number of watt-hours. Once the stored energy is used, it must be recharged.
 When appliances are plugged directly into a power station, it is obvious what is consuming energy. Once normal household circuits are energized, it becomes easier for someone to switch on another light, television, coffee maker, microwave, fan, or appliance without realizing it is drawing from the same battery.
 For that reason, selected-circuit battery backup works best when the household follows an outage load plan.
 Simple outage load rules 
 Keep only essential transfer circuits enabled.
 Avoid running multiple heating or cooking appliances simultaneously.
 Check the power station's output display before adding a large load.
 Leave output headroom for refrigerators, pumps, and motor startup.
 Charge laptops and portable electronics when other large loads are off.
 Turn off unnecessary lights and entertainment equipment during long outages.
 Plan how and when the battery will be recharged if the outage lasts more than one day.
 How to Use a Professionally Installed Transfer-Switch System During an Outage
 The exact sequence must follow the instructions for your specific transfer switch and power source. Once a compatible system has been professionally installed, a typical manual-backup routine looks like this from the homeowner's perspective:
 Confirm the utility outage and check the power station's remaining battery level.
 Turn off or disconnect unnecessary high-demand appliances.
 Connect the power station only through the approved backup-power connection installed for the system.
 Turn on the power station's AC output.
 Operate the transfer equipment according to its manufacturer instructions.
 Bring essential circuits online gradually rather than switching every load on at once.
 Watch the station's output wattage while refrigerators, pumps, blowers, or other motor loads start.
 Disable nonessential circuits if the load approaches the station's rated output.
 Monitor battery percentage and estimated runtime throughout the outage.
 When utility power returns, follow the transfer-switch manufacturer's procedure for returning circuits to utility power before disconnecting the backup source.
 This is an operating overview, not a wiring procedure. Installation, circuit modification, breaker-panel work, neutral changes, inlet installation, and transfer-equipment wiring should be handled by a qualified electrician in accordance with the equipment instructions and applicable local requirements.
 Common Portable Power Station + Transfer Switch Mistakes
 Using a male-to-male cord to backfeed a receptacle
 Never do this. Household receptacles are outputs, not backup-power inlets. Backfeeding can energize wiring unexpectedly and bypass the controlled isolation provided by proper transfer equipment.
 Assuming a 30A transfer switch means you have 30A available
 The power source sets the available power. A 2,400W, 120V source is approximately a 20A source at its rated output, regardless of whether the transfer equipment itself is rated for 30A.
 Buying an L14-30 adapter before checking voltage
 An L14-30 connector is commonly associated with 125/250V generator equipment. A physical adapter does not give a 120V-only power station split-phase 240V capability.
 Trying to energize both sides of the panel from one 120V source
 This can interact with 240V loads, shared-neutral circuits, breaker arrangements, and the transfer equipment itself. Do not improvise this configuration.
 Ignoring motor startup
 A 500W furnace blower, refrigerator compressor, or pump may briefly require substantially more power when it starts. A backup system must satisfy both normal running demand and startup behavior.
 Putting every convenient circuit on backup
 A battery is most useful when it is reserved for priorities. The fewer unnecessary loads you energize, the longer the outage reserve lasts.
 Assuming 240V equipment will work because its wattage looks low
 Voltage comes first. A 1,000W 240V appliance is still a 240V appliance. A 120V portable power station does not become compatible simply because it has more than 1,000W of inverter capacity.
 Forgetting about recharge strategy
 A transfer switch solves distribution, not energy supply. If your essential circuits use 1,500Wh per day but you can only recharge 400Wh per day, the battery reserve will continue shrinking.
 For longer outages, solar can extend runtime when weather and panel size allow. See UDPOWER's solar panel options and the guide Can a Solar Generator Power a House? .
 Transfer Switch vs. Extension Cords: Which Is Better?

 Questions to Ask Your Electrician Before Installation
 You can make the consultation much more productive by bringing the portable power station's specifications and asking specific questions.
 My power station provides 120V only. Which household circuits can safely be backed up?
 Does this transfer switch require 120/240V split-phase input, or can it be configured for my 120V source?
 What inlet and cord arrangement is appropriate for the station's output?
 What is the maximum backup load we should design around?
 Does the transfer switch switch the neutral?
 What is the power station's neutral-to-ground arrangement, and is it compatible with this installation?
 Will existing AFCI or GFCI protection continue operating as required?
 Are any selected circuits multi-wire or shared-neutral circuits?
 Do any desired loads require 240V?
 Can the refrigerator, furnace blower, sump pump, or other motor loads start within the station's rated capability?
 Which circuits should remain excluded so the battery cannot be accidentally overloaded?
 What is the correct homeowner operating sequence when utility power fails and returns?
 When a Portable Power Station Is Not the Right Transfer-Switch Source
 A portable battery may not be the best solution if your outage plan requires:
 central air conditioning;
 large 240V well pumps;
 electric water heating;
 electric resistance heating;
 electric clothes drying;
 full electric-range operation;
 Level 2 EV charging;
 several kilowatts of continuous power for many hours;
 automatic whole-home operation with little or no load management.
 Those situations usually point toward a larger 120/240V split-phase battery system, permanently installed home energy-storage system, appropriately sized fuel generator, or another professionally designed backup solution.
 If you are trying to understand how much power a home actually uses before choosing a backup system, read How Many Watts Does a House Use? .
 When a Portable Power Station Makes Excellent Sense
 A portable battery becomes much more attractive when the goal is modest and clearly defined:
 keep food refrigerated;
 keep internet and phones available;
 maintain basic lighting;
 support compatible medical or comfort equipment;
 operate a compatible 120V furnace blower;
 run a 120V sump pump intermittently;
 avoid gasoline, fumes, engine noise, and outdoor generator operation;
 use the same battery for camping, RV travel, job-site power, and emergencies.
 Unlike a fuel generator, a battery power station can also be used indoors because it has no combustion engine or exhaust. For more on that distinction, see Indoor Generator Guide: Safe Home Backup Power .
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can any portable power station connect to a transfer switch?
 No. The station's voltage, rated output, AC outlet, neutral and grounding arrangement, protective devices, and manufacturer requirements all need to match the transfer equipment and selected household circuits.
 Can I connect a 120V portable power station to a 240V transfer switch?
 Do not assume that you can. Many traditional 30A generator transfer switches are designed for 120/240V split-phase sources. A 120V-only station does not provide the second hot leg needed for normal 240V operation. A licensed electrician must determine whether the specific transfer equipment supports an approved 120V-only configuration.
 Can an adapter turn a 120V power station into a 240V source?
 No. An adapter can change connector shapes or wiring interfaces, but it cannot create true 120/240V split-phase output from a source that only produces 120V.
 Can I power both sides of my breaker panel from a 120V power station?
 Do not attempt to do this with an improvised adapter. Residential panels can contain 240V loads, shared-neutral circuits, and other wiring arrangements that require proper source and transfer-equipment design. Have an electrician identify which 120V circuits can be backed up safely.
 Can a portable power station run a furnace through a transfer switch?
 Potentially. Many gas-furnace blowers and controls use 120V, but the circuit is often hardwired and the motor may have significant startup demand. A properly installed 120V transfer solution can be useful when the furnace voltage, starting load, controls, grounding, and transfer equipment are compatible.
 Can a portable power station run a well pump through a transfer switch?
 It depends on the pump. Some pumps use 120V while many deep-well pumps use 240V. A 120V-only station such as the UDPOWER S1200 or S2400 cannot directly supply a 240V pump. Even a 120V pump must be checked for startup current.
 Can I run central air conditioning from the UDPOWER S2400 through a transfer switch?
 No for a typical 208/240V central air-conditioning system. The S2400 provides 120V AC output and does not provide 240V split-phase power. Some smaller 120V window or portable air conditioners may be possible when their running and startup demands fit within the station's capabilities.
 Does a 30A transfer switch mean the S2400 can supply 30 amps?
 No. The S2400 is rated at 2,400W at 120V, which is approximately 20A at rated output. A higher-rated switch does not increase the output available from the power station.
 Is a transfer switch better than running extension cords?
 It depends on the goal. Direct appliance connection is cheaper and simpler. A transfer switch is more convenient when you need selected built-in circuits or hardwired 120V equipment, but installation costs more and requires much more compatibility planning.
 Can I backfeed my house through a wall outlet during an outage?
 No. Do not connect a portable power station or generator to an ordinary household outlet to feed power backward into the home's wiring. Use appropriately designed transfer equipment installed for the purpose.
 Should I use surge watts when sizing the transfer switch?
 Use the power station's rated continuous output as the primary load-planning limit. Startup or higher-power capability matters for motors and compressors, but it should not replace the rated output when deciding how much normal household load the backup source should carry.
 Does a transfer switch make the battery last longer?
 No. It only changes how power reaches the loads. Runtime still depends on battery capacity and actual energy consumption. In fact, panel-connected circuits can make it easier to consume more energy unless the household follows a load-management plan.
 Can a portable power station automatically take over when the grid fails?
 Only when the power station and transfer equipment are specifically designed for that function. A manual transfer switch requires manual operation. A power station's built-in UPS feature for devices plugged directly into the unit should not be confused with automatic transfer of household circuits.
 Bottom Line
 Yes, a portable power station can be used with a transfer switch, but compatibility is determined by the electrical system—not simply by battery size. 
 For a 120V-only power station, the most sensible goal is usually a carefully selected group of 120V essential circuits. Voltage, rated output, connector type, neutral and ground configuration, branch-circuit arrangement, motor startup demand, and transfer-switch design all need to agree.
 For UDPOWER specifically, the S2400's 2,083Wh battery and 2,400W rated output make it the strongest current option for substantial 120V essential-load backup. However, it is still a 120V portable power station rather than a native 120/240V whole-home battery system. Direct appliance use remains the simplest approach, while any transfer-switch installation should be reviewed and installed by a qualified electrician.

 Start with the loads that actually matter during an outage, then choose the battery capacity and output that can support them without paying for power you will never use.

Transfer Switches for Portable Power Stations | Outlet Powered 
 Skip to content Quick answer
 You only need a transfer switch for a portable power station if you want it to supply household circuits; appliances plugged into its own outlets don't need one. For circuits, the options are a manual transfer switch, a panelboard interlock kit with an inlet, or a compatible manufacturer home-backup panel, assessed and installed by a licensed electrician with any required permit. A 120V-only station can't supply 240V circuits.
 Safety first
 This is general information, not electrical advice. Never connect a power station or generator to a wall outlet or your panel with a double-ended ("male to male") cord: it can energize utility lines and injure line workers. Connecting to home circuits needs listed transfer equipment installed by a licensed electrician with any required permit. Follow the maker's manual and your local code.
 Why home circuits need transfer equipment
 You don't need a transfer switch for a portable power station when you plug a refrigerator, router or other compatible appliance into its built-in outlets, as its manual allows. Feeding electricity through your home's existing circuits is different. Those circuits normally get power from the utility, and an alternate source must never be accidentally interconnected with the utility supply. Transfer equipment provides that isolation.
 NEC Article 702 covers optional standby systems, including portable generators connected to premises wiring. Its transfer-equipment requirements call for equipment designed and installed to prevent inadvertent interconnection of normal utility power and an alternate power source. Which requirements apply depends on the code edition adopted in your area, and some areas still use an older NEC edition. Your licensed electrician has to identify the applicable rules, equipment requirements and permits before installation.
 Planning-level transfer equipment options
 A portable backup system can be set up to supply selected household circuits in a few ways. The right one depends on your electrical panel, backup power source, intended circuits and equipment compatibility.
 Manual transfer switch
 A manual transfer switch gives you a controlled way to choose between utility power and an alternate source for the circuits it serves. Transfer switches are evaluated to UL 1008. A manual switch is one option when you want to supply selected essential circuits during an outage. Your electrician decides whether a proposed switch suits your electrical system, backup source and loads, and it has to be compatible with the power station's electrical output. A switch advertised for a fuel generator won't automatically work with every battery power station.
 Panelboard interlock kit with an inlet
 An interlock kit is another transfer-equipment arrangement. Breaker interlock kits are evaluated as part of the panelboard under UL 67, and the panelboard must be marked for the specific kit; a kit that merely appears to fit isn't evidence of compatibility. Your electrician verifies the panelboard marking, the approved equipment, the backup source and the applicable electrical requirements, and confirms that the inlet and associated transfer equipment suit the system. This is a professional electrical installation, not a plug-in accessory that removes the need for an electrician.
 Manufacturer home-backup panels
 Some power station manufacturers sell smart panels, home-backup panels or other accessories that link compatible battery equipment to selected home circuits. Compatibility is model-specific: a panel from the same manufacturer isn't automatically compatible with everything that company sells. Before choosing one, confirm its supported power stations, electrical ratings, intended circuits and installation requirements. Your electrician still assesses and installs the complete arrangement, and the accessory doesn't remove the need for listed transfer equipment, applicable permits or safe isolation from utility power.
 Understanding 120V and 120/240V backup
 Voltage is a separate question from battery capacity. A large battery can store a lot of energy while providing only 120V AC output, and that doesn't make it a 240V backup source. Some household equipment needs 240V, and a 120V-only station can't supply a 240V circuit just because it has a large inverter or battery. Our manufacturer specification table includes these examples:

 Inlet voltage and compatibility
 The inlet and transfer equipment have to match the backup arrangement approved for the home, and a 120/240V system has different requirements from a 120V-only one. Adapters, connector appearance and matching outlet shapes don't establish electrical compatibility. Your electrician verifies that the power station, inlet, transfer equipment and intended circuits work together, taking into account the equipment's output limits and the loads the backup source is expected to carry. For systems that include pumps, read our well pump backup guide .
 Essential circuits or the entire house
 Installing transfer equipment doesn't mean your battery can power every appliance. Essential-circuit backup focuses on selected loads, which depending on the household might be refrigeration, lighting, communications or heating-system controls. Whole-house coverage can involve more circuits and higher simultaneous demand. Either way, battery capacity and continuous output have to be checked separately. For example, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 has:
 Rated capacity: 4,096Wh
 Continuous AC output: 4,000W
 Surge rating: 8,000W
 Output: 120/240V
 Those output ratings don't tell you how long it can carry your household; runtime depends on the energy the connected appliances use. Run your loads through our size calculator before settling on the scope of an installation, and read whole-house battery backup for a broader comparison.
 What to ask your licensed electrician
 Before buying transfer equipment or accessories, go through these questions with your electrician and have them confirm compatibility:
 Which household circuits are intended for backup?
 Which loads require 120V or 240V?
 What are the appliances' running and startup requirements?
 Is the selected power station compatible with those loads?
 Is a manual transfer switch suitable for the home?
 Is the existing panelboard marked for a compatible interlock kit?
 Would a manufacturer home-backup panel be appropriate?
 Which equipment and inlet ratings are required?
 Which NEC edition and local requirements apply?
 What permits and inspections are required?
 Don't plan household circuit backup on a product's maximum output rating alone.
 What renters can do instead
 Renters may not be able to authorize changes to the home's electrical panel, but a portable power station can still run compatible appliances from its built-in outlets without touching household circuits. Pick the appliances you can power directly, check their electrical requirements, and estimate the battery capacity you need. Our home backup guide covers that appliance-level planning.
 Questions readers ask
 Do I need a transfer switch for a portable power station?
 Not when you plug compatible appliances straight into the station's built-in outlets. Supplying home circuits requires listed transfer equipment installed by a licensed electrician with any required permit.
 Is a transfer switch different from an interlock kit?
 Yes. Transfer switches are evaluated to UL 1008. Breaker interlock kits are evaluated as part of the panelboard under UL 67, and the panel must be marked for the specific kit.
 Can a 120V power station supply 240V home circuits?
 No. A 120V-only power station doesn't provide native 240V output. Your licensed electrician must verify voltage compatibility between the power source, transfer equipment and intended circuits.
 Can I install home-backup equipment myself?
 No. Connecting a portable power source to household circuits requires a licensed electrician and any required permit. Renters and homeowners can instead plug compatible appliances directly into the station's built-in outlets without modifying household wiring.

 Portable Power Stations and EVs as Home Backup: What They Run and How They Connect
 What a 5 kWh power station or an electric truck runs in an outage, the three ways to connect one to your panel, and which vehicles can back up a house.
 By Eastside Electrical & HVAC 
 Published October 22, 2026 
 Sources checked 2026-10-22 
 Six days after the November 2024 windstorm, about 18,000 Puget Sound Energy (PSE) customers in North King County were still without power. A portable power station, or an electric vehicle that can power a house, will keep a refrigerator, the internet and a gas furnace's fan running for a night or for several days, depending on the size of its battery. How long it lasts comes down to its stored energy and what you plug in, and whether it can feed your house wiring comes down to the equipment between the battery and your panel, which has to keep its power off the utility's lines.
 Source: Puget Sound Energy, Power restored to nearly all PSE customers , November 25, 2024, customers remaining without power in North King County after the previous Tuesday's windstorm. 
 Kilowatt-hours set how long a station lasts, and watts set what it can run
 A portable power station is a large rechargeable battery with an inverter , the electronics that turn stored battery power into the same 120-volt or 240-volt power your outlets deliver. Four figures on its spec sheet decide what it can do for the house:
 Stored energy, in watt-hours (Wh) or kilowatt-hours (kWh). One kWh is 1,000 watts, a kilowatt (kW), used for one hour.
 Continuous output, in watts: the most it can supply at once. Everything switched on together has to stay under it.
 Surge, in watts: the brief extra power it can give a motor in the moment it starts.
 Voltage. A station with 240-volt output can run 240-volt equipment, such as a 240-volt well pump; a 120-volt-only station cannot.
 The last column is the safety listing each maker states: the standard a testing laboratory such as UL has checked the product against.

 UL 9540 is the safety standard for energy storage systems and equipment, and UL 1973 is a standard for batteries in stationary use. Where a spec page names no listing, the label on the unit settles it.
 Five kilowatt-hours runs a refrigerator for days and a sump pump for hours
 Divide a station's stored watt-hours by the watts a load draws and you have its hours, the way the makers figure it: Goal Zero says a refrigerator averaging 55 watts runs about 72 hours on its Yeti PRO 4000. The inverter uses a little of the energy itself, so real hours come in somewhat lower. On one 5,040 Wh Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus, one load at a time:

 One load at a time; loads sharing the battery, and the inverter's own use, shorten every bar. 
 The furnace, sump pump and well pump rows assume a motor that never stops; those motors usually run only part of the time, so their real hours stretch longer. Loads that share the battery add up fast: the refrigerator, internet and lights (115 watts) plus a gas furnace whose 800-watt blower runs half of each hour (400 watts on average) come to about 515 watts, and 5,040 Wh lasts about 10 hours. For a gas-heated house, a 5 kWh station is a bridge through one cold night. What each heating system draws, and why heat strips and baseboard heaters are beyond a station, is in our guide to keeping the heat on in an outage .
 A well pump belongs on the list only if the station's voltage matches the pump's nameplate and its surge rating covers the start, which Champion's generator chart puts at 1,500 to 2,000 watts for a half-horsepower pump and 2,000 to 4,000 watts for a 1-horsepower pump. Both 7,200-watt stations above publish 240-volt output and surge ratings above that; check the maker's figures against your pump's label before you count on it. Leave the electric water heater, range, dryer and car charging off a station, and plan any medical equipment with its maker; our standby generator and home battery comparison covers medical loads.
 Source: Champion Power Equipment, Generator Wattage Chart , half- and 1-horsepower well pump starting watts. Checked October 22, 2026. 
 Three ways to connect a power station to the house
 A station's own outlets reach only what plugs into them. Feeding the house wiring takes transfer equipment . The 2023 National Electrical Code (NEC), which Washington enforces until the 2026 edition takes over for permits issued from December 31, 2026, requires it to be listed , tested by a safety laboratory and marked for the job, and built so the backup source and the utility can never be connected at the same time (section 702.5(A)). The rule for which code edition applies has exceptions for new one- and two-family or multifamily dwellings with earlier building permits, and for new installations whose required plans were received and accepted for review before that date. The code's standby rules cover a portable power supply connected to house wiring, not only a generator (section 702.1).
 Code: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code , 2023 edition, §702.1, systems arranged for connection to premises wiring from a portable alternate power supply, and §702.5(A), listed transfer equipment that prevents interconnection of sources, as adopted by WAC 296-46B-010(1) , with the 2026 edition for permits issued on or after December 31, 2026. 
 Only the second and third routes reach wired-in loads such as a furnace or well pump. 
 Cords to the appliances
 The simplest setup needs no electrician. Plug the refrigerator, a lamp and the modem and router straight into the station, and a corded sump pump straight in, without an extension cord, as our sump pump guide explains. Where a cord has to reach, the gauge-and-length rules in our extension cord guide decide which one, and no cord runs through a wall. The limit is everything wired in place: a gas furnace, a well pump, ceiling lights and a garage door opener have no plug to use.
 An inlet with a transfer switch or interlock
 This is the hookup a portable generator uses. An electrician mounts a power inlet , a box with a socket for one heavy cord, and wires it to a manual transfer switch , a small panel that moves a chosen set of circuits to backup power, or to an interlock , a sliding plate on the main panel that lets the main breaker (the switch that shuts off the whole panel) or the backup breaker be on, never both. One cord runs from the station's 240-volt outlet to the inlet; the Jackery 5000 Plus, for example, has a 30-amp NEMA L14-30 (amps measure electric current), the twist-lock socket many portable generators use, and Jackery says it can connect to a house through a transfer switch or an inlet box. A 30-amp inlet carries up to about 7,200 watts, as our portable generator hookup page explains, the continuous output of the two largest stations above. With manual equipment the code lets you choose what to switch on (section 702.4(A)(1)), so the station carries only what is on at one time.
 Two details carry over from generators. The station's neutral , the return wire, is either bonded (tied to ground inside the unit) or floating (not tied), and the transfer equipment has to be wired to match, with a sign at the inlet saying which (section 702.7(C)); Anker says the inlet box or transfer switch needs its neutral and ground wires properly connected. An interlock must be the kit listed for your panel's make and model, as our heating backup guide explains. The code puts a portable generator's inlet outdoors (section 702.12(B)); for a battery that stays indoors, the inspector decides where the inlet may go.
 Sources: Jackery, Explorer 5000 Plus , NEMA L14-30 outlet and connection through a transfer switch or inlet box; Anker SOLIX, 10-Circuit Manual Transfer Switch , neutral and ground check; NFPA 70, National Electrical Code , 2023 edition, §702.4(A)(1), user-selected loads, §702.7(C), inlet sign for bonded or floating neutral, and §702.12(B), inlet outside the building for portable generators of 15 kW or less. 
 The maker's own transfer panel
 Most large stations have a matching panel from their maker. It mounts beside the main panel as a subpanel , a second breaker box fed from the main one; the electrician moves the circuits you choose into it, and the station plugs into it with the maker's cable. Some switch over on their own in 20 milliseconds, a fiftieth of a second, so the refrigerator and the internet never notice the outage.

 UL 1008 is the safety standard for transfer switches. EcoFlow's panel is fed from a 100-amp breaker in your main panel, has a sliding interlock between its utility and generator main breakers, takes a 3 to 12 kW generator as a second source, and does not replace your main breaker. BLUETTI's AT1 Smart Distribution Panel, for its Apex 300 and EnergyPro batteries, lists four UL standards in its manual, among them UL 67 for panels and UL 1741 for equipment that ties batteries and solar into house wiring.
 We connect only listed transfer equipment and maker panels bought through manufacturer or distributor supply. Before we wire one in, we check the listing mark on the panel itself against the certifier's directory; a kit whose listing we cannot verify, we do not install. Our UL versus ETL guide shows how to check a mark yourself.
 A double-plug cord into a wall outlet is never a hookup
 Plugging a station's output into a wall outlet, or into the dryer outlet, with a cord that has a plug on each end is backfeeding : power pushed into the house wiring with nothing to stop it flowing back out onto the utility's lines. In March 2026 the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) told consumers to stop using and throw away these male-to-male cords, whose exposed prongs can become live and cause electrocution or fire. A battery is no safer for being quiet; our power outage checklist explains the danger to line crews.
 Sources: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, CPSC Warns Consumers to Stop Using Male-to-Male Extension Cords , release 26-363, March 31, 2026, exposed prongs, electrocution, fire and backfeeding. 
 A power station can sit indoors, but the storage rules depend on the inspector
 A station has no engine and no exhaust, so unlike a portable generator it can stay inside. Jackery says its 5000 Plus "can run inside with confidence," and Goal Zero says the Yeti PRO 4000 can be used safely inside your home. The garage beside the panel is the usual spot, within two limits the makers set:
 Temperature. Jackery's 5000 Plus charges only between 32°F and 113°F and runs down to 5°F; EcoFlow's DELTA Pro Ultra runs down to 4°F below zero and warms its own battery below freezing. A station in an unheated garage during a cold snap may not recharge until it warms up.
 A dry, clear wall. Jackery's Smart Transfer Switch has to be indoors or out of the rain. EcoFlow's battery connection box is indoor-only, its panel goes where it is safe from flooding and away from stored flammable materials, and it needs 3 feet of clear space in front.
 Sources: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, CPSC Warns of Generator, Carbon Monoxide and Fire Hazards , release 26-519, May 27, 2026, generators outdoors only; Jackery, Explorer 5000 Plus , indoor use and charge and discharge temperatures; Goal Zero, Yeti PRO 4000 , indoor use; EcoFlow, DELTA Pro Ultra , operating temperature and self-heating; Jackery, Smart Transfer Switch , indoor installation; EcoFlow, Smart Home Panel 2 Installation Guide , indoor battery connection box, flooding, flammable materials and front clearance. 
 Whether the code treats your station as a portable source or as a permanent battery matters at permit time. Beyond the standby rules for portable sources, the electrical code treats devices "installed as a system" that store energy and feed the house wiring as an energy storage system , which its Article 706 covers above 1 kWh. Washington's residential code requires a home energy storage system to be listed and labeled for residential use to UL 9540, and to be commissioned before use: checked against its approved plans, with the maker's instructions left with the owner and a service contact label on the system. Whether a permit office applies those rules to a wheeled station plugged into its panel is the office's call, so ask before you buy. A UL 9540 listing answers the listing question either way.
 Sources: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code , 2023 edition, Article 100, definition of energy storage system, §702.1, scope, and §706.1, energy storage systems above 1 kWh; Washington State Legislature, WAC 51-51-0328 , Washington amendments to IRC section R328, R328.2 UL 9540 listing for residential use and R328.12 commissioning, effective March 15, 2024. 
 Sun, a generator or a truck can refill a station in a long outage
 When the power comes back, the big stations refill fast from the wall: Goal Zero says its Yeti PRO 4000 goes from empty to 80 percent in 2 hours at 1,800 watts, and Jackery lists 3.5 hours for the 5000 Plus on its wall adapter. Through a multi-day outage, three other sources can refill one:
 Solar panels. Goal Zero says 3,000 watts of panels take the Yeti PRO 4000 from empty to 80 percent in under 90 minutes, and Jackery lists 6.5 to 8.5 hours of solar charging for the 5000 Plus. A winter storm may give too little sun to refill a battery, as our generator, solar and battery comparison explains.
 A gas generator. Jackery and EcoFlow say their stations can charge from one, though Jackery says the 5000 Plus cannot charge through its 120-volt input while it is connected to the Smart Transfer Switch. The generator itself follows every outdoor rule in our power outage checklist .
 A truck's outlets. A truck with household outlets, such as a Ford F-150 Lightning or PowerBoost hybrid with Pro Power Onboard, can feed a station's charging input like a wall outlet. Do not count on a car's 12-volt socket without checking: Jackery lists no car charging for the 5000 Plus.
 Sources: Goal Zero, Yeti PRO 4000 , AC and solar charging; Jackery, Explorer 5000 Plus , AC adapter and solar charging times, generator charging, no 120-volt charging while connected to the Smart Transfer Switch, and no 12-volt car adapter; EcoFlow, DELTA Pro Ultra , generator charging; Ford, Home Backup Power , Pro Power Onboard on the F-150 Lightning and PowerBoost hybrid. 
 A vehicle powers a house only through a bidirectional charger and a transfer device
 Vehicle-to-home, or V2H , uses the car's battery the way a power station uses its own, with far more energy. The car connects through a bidirectional charger , one that sends power out of the car as well as into it, and a transfer device that disconnects the house from the utility before the car feeds it. The electrical code requires charging equipment that exports power to be listed and marked for that purpose and applies its standby rules when it backs up a house (section 625.48); the code's note points to UL 9741, the standard for bidirectional EV charging equipment. Washington's residential code exempts a car's own battery from its storage-system listing rule on the same condition: the installation follows section 625.48.
 Sources: NFPA 70, National Electrical Code , 2023 edition, §625.48 and Informational Note No. 2, interactive equipment listed and marked, Parts I and II of Article 702 for optional standby, and UL 9741; Washington State Legislature, WAC 51-51-0328 , R328.2 Exception 2, vehicle batteries under NEC 625.48.

 The truck feeds the house only through its bidirectional charger, after the transfer device beside the panel has disconnected the house from the utility. 
 Tesla. Of Tesla's vehicles, only the Cybertruck can back up a house that has no Powerwall. Once Powershare is on, the truck starts feeding the house on its own when the grid drops, and the house may lose power briefly at the switch. In a house with a Powerwall, Tesla also lets Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered in the U.S. after October 1, 2026, and some built earlier, back it up. You set a discharge limit in the Tesla app, the charge level where the truck stops feeding the house, and the truck's own outlets are off while it does.
 GM. The PowerShift Charger charges at up to 80 amps, or 19.2 kW. For backup it pairs with the V2H Enablement Kit: a Home Hub that disconnects the house from the grid, for homes whose electrical service (the utility connection) is up to 200 amps; a 9.6 kW inverter that turns the truck's battery power into household power; and a small "dark start" battery that wakes the system in a blackout. Some 2024 vehicles need a software update first, and owners turn on automatic backup in GM's EV dashboard.
 Ford. Ford's Charge Station Pro backs up a house only with Ford's Home Integration System installed. The newer route runs a cord from the truck's 240-volt Pro Power Onboard outlet to a GenerLink transfer switch at or beside the meter, and you plug the truck in when the power goes out. The electrical code requires a transfer switch mounted between the meter and its socket to be a listed meter-mounted type the inspector approves (section 702.5(B)), and Ford says GenerLink needs your utility's approval. The truck's outlet itself must be listed, rated no more than 250 volts and 50 amps, and protected inside the vehicle against overloads and shocks (section 625.60).
 Kia. Backup needs the Wallbox Power Recovery Unit as well as the Quasar 2 charger. Kia's owner page says the equipment has to sit in a garage or carport with shade and ventilation, and the car must stay above 20 percent charge.

 A bidirectional charger is also the car's everyday charger, and a big one: an 80-amp charger needs a 100-amp circuit, as our EV charger types guide shows. Our load management guide covers whether your panel and service can carry it, and our EV charger installation cost guide what the circuit costs.
 Get the vehicle warranty answer in writing first
 None of the four makers' backup pages we read says whether powering a house affects the vehicle's battery warranty; the warranties we read cover only the home equipment. Tesla's Powershare Home Backup Limited Warranty covers the Powershare Gateway and Backup Switch for 10 years and the Universal Wall Connector for 4, GM gives each V2H kit part 10 years and the PowerShift Charger 3, and Ford backs Charge Station Pro for 3. Ask the dealer for the answer in writing, for your vehicle, before you rely on it to run the house.

 Switch the house over once before the storm
 Before you accept the job, these should all be true:
 The backed-up circuits run from the battery. With the utility side switched off, the chosen circuits come on from the station or vehicle, and nothing else does.
 The two sources cannot meet. The interlock or transfer switch blocks the utility and the battery from being on together.
 The neutral matches. The sign at any inlet says bonded or floating, and it matches the station's setting.
 Every backed-up circuit is labeled, with the total watts the station or vehicle can carry written at the panel.
 Automatic systems switch over and back. A test outage moves the house to the battery and back on its own, and the reserve is set, such as the discharge limit in Tesla's app.
 The refill plan works. The solar panels, generator or truck outlet you plan to use actually charges the station.
 You have the paperwork: the listing labels and model numbers, the maker's instructions and the permit approval.
